title: Development of novel benzo[ d ][1,2,3]triazole-acetohydrazone derivatives as potential therapeutic agents: synthesis, SAR study, inhibition of carbohydrate metabolism enzymes, and aldose reductase supported by molecular modelling simulation
content: Diabetes prevalence is on the rise worldwide, which makes it more urgent to develop safe, effective, and multi-targeted inhibitors. Herein, we describe the synthesis of novel bioactive benzo[d][1,2,3]triazole-acetohydrazone derivatives 4–12. These compounds were prepared via condensation reactions between benzotriazole-carbohydrazide and various formyl benzylidene derivatives, 4-formyl-1,3-diarylpyrazole, and cyclic ketones (ninhydrin and 2,3-dioxoindole), all of which are linked through an acetohydrazone moiety. The structures of derivatives 4–12 were confirmed using FT-IR, NMR (1H/13C{1H}) spectroscopy, elemental analysis, and HPLC. The synthesized analogues were assessed for their ability to mitigate hyperglycemia by inhibiting carbohydrate-metabolizing enzymes (α-amylase and α-glucosidase) and suppressing aldose reductase in the polyol pathway. Compound 11 exhibited particularly notable efficacy, demonstrating IC50 values of 6.08 ± 0.06 µg mL−1 for α-amylase and 5.01 ± 0.09 µg mL−1 for α-glucosidase. These values are comparable to those of acarbose (IC50 = 5.54 ± 0.04 µg mL−1 for α-amylase and IC50 = 4.53 ± 0.06 µg mL−1 for α-glucosidase). SAR analysis indicated that the presence of two carbonyl groups and a hydrophobic aromatic ring is crucial for synergistic activity in compound 11. Furthermore, compounds 6–12 displayed significant aldose reductase inhibitory activity, with IC50 values below 10 µg mL−1, and compound 11 demonstrated the most potent activity, with an IC50 value of 4.07 ± 0.10 µg mL−1, which closely approached that of quercetin (IC50 = 3.68 ± 0.11 µg mL−1). Consequently, compound 11 holds promise as a lead molecule for developing novel therapeutic agents targeting α-amylase, α-glucosidase, and aldose reductase for diabetes management. Furthermore, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations (100 ns) elucidated stable interactions between compound 11 and the catalytic pockets of both α-amylase and α-glucosidase, primarily mediated by hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. The ADME analysis revealed an acceptable physicochemical profile, characterized by good aqueous solubility and a minimal predicted risk of CYP-mediated drug–drug interaction. Finally, these findings indicate that benzotriazole derivative 11 may serve as a promising scaffold for further optimization toward a multi-target anti-diabetic drug development agent.
